title: ELAN — timing of anticoagulation after AF-associated stroke
headline: Early DOAC: composite 2.9 vs 4.1% (difference not significant)
question: How did earlier DOAC initiation compare with a later schedule?
population: 2,013 people with acute ischemic stroke and atrial fibrillation.
comparison: Earlier: within 48 hours for minor/moderate stroke or days 6–7 for major stroke. Later: days 3–4, 6–7 or 12–14, respectively.
result: The 30-day composite of recurrent ischemic stroke, systemic embolism, major extracranial bleeding, symptomatic intracranial hemorrhage or vascular death was 2.9% versus 4.1% (risk difference −1.18 percentage points; 95% CI −2.84 to 0.47). Symptomatic intracranial hemorrhage was 0.2% in both groups.
limits: The confidence interval includes no difference. Trial severity categories and exclusions require review; this is not an automatic start-date rule.

title: OPTIMAS — early versus delayed DOAC initiation
headline: DOAC ≤4 days noninferior to days 7–14 (3.3% each)
question: Was initiation within four days noninferior to starting at 7–14 days?
population: 3,621 analyzed adults with AF-associated ischemic stroke at 100 UK hospitals; clinicians were uncertain about timing.
comparison: DOAC initiation within four days versus days 7–14.
result: At 90 days, recurrent ischemic stroke, symptomatic intracranial hemorrhage, unclassifiable stroke or systemic embolism occurred in 3.3% of each group. Noninferiority met the two-percentage-point margin; superiority was not demonstrated. Symptomatic intracranial hemorrhage was 0.6% versus 0.7%.
limits: Open-label treatment with masked adjudication. Apply the trial selection criteria; identical observed rates do not prove identical individual risk.

result: At 30 days, recurrent ischemic stroke, symptomatic intracerebral hemorrhage or unclassified stroke occurred in 2.1% versus 3.0% (OR 0.70; 95% CI 0.50–0.98). Symptomatic intracerebral hemorrhage was 0.4% in each group.

population: 4,881 patients with minor ischemic stroke or high-risk TIA at international sites.
comparison: Clopidogrel plus aspirin versus aspirin alone for the 90-day trial period.

question: Does thrombectomy improve outcome after a primary isolated medium or distal occlusion?

headline: Early MIS (mainly lobar): utility-weighted mRS 0.458 vs 0.374
question: Does early minimally invasive evacuation improve recovery after selected ICH?
population: 300 patients with lobar or anterior basal ganglia ICH of 30–80 mL; treatment assignment within 24 hours.

title: ANNEXA-I — hemostatic efficacy and thrombotic harm
headline: Andexanet: hemostasis 67.0 vs 53.1%; thrombotic events 10.3 vs 5.6%
question: What were andexanet’s efficacy and safety tradeoffs in factor Xa inhibitor-associated ICH?
population: 530 patients with acute ICH after factor Xa inhibitor use within 15 hours; the interim efficacy analysis included 452.
comparison: Andexanet versus usual care; 85.5% of usual-care patients received PCC.
result: Composite hemostatic efficacy was 67.0% versus 53.1% (adjusted difference 13.4 percentage points; 95% CI 4.6–22.2). Thrombotic events occurred in 10.3% versus 5.6%, including ischemic stroke in 6.5% versus 1.5%. No appreciable difference in 30-day mRS or mortality was reported.
limits: Hemostatic efficacy is not functional benefit. NCS/SCCM 2026 conditionally recommends 4F-PCC rather than andexanet, and andexanet was withdrawn from the US market effective 22 December 2025.

headline: DOAC after ICH: fewer ischemic strokes, more recurrent ICH
question: How did DOACs change ischemic and hemorrhagic stroke risk after ICH?

title: PROGRESS — blood-pressure lowering after stroke or TIA

question: Did a perindopril-based regimen reduce recurrent stroke?
population: 6,105 people with previous stroke/TIA, including hypertensive and non-hypertensive participants.
comparison: Perindopril-based treatment, with indapamide at clinician discretion, versus matching placebo.

headline: Mechanical valves: dabigatran worse than warfarin
question: Could dabigatran replace warfarin after mechanical valve replacement?
population: 252 participants with mechanical aortic or mitral valves, either implanted within seven days or at least three months earlier.
comparison: Kidney-function- and concentration-adjusted dabigatran versus warfarin.
result: This phase 2 study, whose primary endpoint was dabigatran trough concentration, stopped early for excess thromboembolism and bleeding. In the as-treated analysis, ischemic or unspecified stroke occurred in nine dabigatran recipients versus none with warfarin; major bleeding occurred in seven versus two.
limits: A dose-validation study with adverse clinical outcomes, not a successful clinical noninferiority trial. Findings in ordinary AF cannot be transferred to mechanical valves.

title: PROACT Xa — apixaban in an On-X mechanical aortic valve
headline: On-X valve: apixaban worse than warfarin
question: Was apixaban noninferior to warfarin with this mechanical aortic valve?
population: 863 participants with an On-X mechanical aortic valve implanted at least three months earlier; 94% also took aspirin.
comparison: Apixaban versus warfarin targeting INR 2.0–3.0.
result: Stopped early for excess thromboembolic events. Valve thrombosis or valve-related thromboembolism occurred at 4.2% versus 1.3% per patient-year (rate difference 2.9 percentage points per year; 95% CI 0.8–5.0), failing noninferiority. Major bleeding was 3.6% versus 4.5% per patient-year.
limits: These are event rates, not percentages of participants: 20 events occurred in 16 apixaban recipients versus six events in six warfarin recipients. Results do not support replacing warfarin with apixaban in this valve population.

title: INTERACT2 — acute ICH blood-pressure lowering
headline: ICH SBP <140: primary outcome NS (OR 0.87); ordinal shift favored
question: Did early intensive BP lowering improve 90-day function?
population: 2,839 patients with spontaneous ICH within six hours and elevated systolic BP; 2,794 had primary-outcome data.
comparison: SBP target <140 mmHg within one hour versus <180 mmHg, using clinician-selected agents.
result: Death or major disability (mRS 3–6) was 52.0% versus 55.6% (OR 0.87; 95% CI 0.75–1.01; P=0.06). The prespecified ordinal analysis favored intensive treatment (OR for greater disability 0.87; 95% CI 0.77–1.00; P=0.04). Mortality was 11.9% versus 12.0%; nonfatal serious adverse events were similar.
limits: The dichotomous primary outcome was not statistically significant. Distinguish the tested early ICH strategy from post-EVT BP targets and from more aggressive lowering in ATACH-2.

title: ATACH-2 — intensive BP lowering and renal adverse events
headline: ICH SBP 110–139: no benefit; renal events 9.0 vs 4.0%
question: Was an SBP target of 110–139 better than 140–179 mmHg?
population: 1,000 patients with acute ICH <60 cm³ and GCS ≥5; IV nicardipine began within 4.5 hours of symptom onset.
comparison: SBP target 110–139 versus 140–179 mmHg.
result: Death or disability (mRS 4–6) at three months was 38.7% versus 37.7% (adjusted RR 1.04; 95% CI 0.85–1.27). Renal adverse events within seven days were more frequent with intensive treatment: 9.0% versus 4.0% (P=0.002).
limits: Stopped for futility. The selected volume/GCS population and different BP targets limit comparison with INTERACT2; these results do not support pushing all acute ICH patients to the lower tested range.

title: INTERACT3 — coordinated acute ICH care bundle
headline: ICH care bundle: better mRS (cOR 0.86)
question: Did implementing a coordinated physiological-care bundle improve function?
population: 7,036 adults with spontaneous ICH within six hours at 121 hospitals in ten countries; 6,255 had primary-outcome data.
comparison: Hospital implementation of early BP lowering, glucose and temperature management, and warfarin reversal for abnormal values versus usual care; stepped-wedge cluster randomization.
result: At six months the bundle improved the ordinal mRS distribution (common OR for worse outcome 0.86; 95% CI 0.76–0.97). Serious adverse events occurred in 16.0% versus 20.1%.
limits: A hospital-level implementation trial, predominantly in low- and middle-income settings with inconsistent existing protocols. Benefit cannot be assigned to BP lowering or another single component; missing outcomes and site withdrawals require attention.

title: FASTEST — recombinant factor VIIa within 2 hours of ICH
headline: rFVIIa: less growth (−3.7 mL), no functional benefit; more thromboembolism
question: Does recombinant factor VIIa within 2 hours improve outcome after spontaneous ICH?
population: 626 adults aged 18–80 with ICH 2–60 mL, limited IVH, GCS ≥8, treated within 2 hours.
comparison: Recombinant factor VIIa 80 µg/kg versus placebo.
result: No difference in 180-day mRS (adjusted cOR 1.09; 95% CI 0.79–1.51); stopped for futility. Life-threatening thromboembolism within 4 days: RR 3.41 (1.14–10.15). ICH growth was 3.7 mL less at 24 hours.
limits: Excluded recent anticoagulation and large hematomas; slowed growth did not translate into function.

title: ENCHANTED2/MT — avoid extrapolating aggressive post-EVT BP lowering
headline: Post-EVT SBP <120: worse outcome (OR 1.37)
question: What happened with SBP <120 after successful thrombectomy?
population: 821 randomized adults in China with persistent SBP ≥140 mmHg after successful reperfusion for intracranial large-vessel occlusion; 810 had primary-outcome data.
comparison: SBP <120 versus 140–180 mmHg, reached within one hour and maintained for 72 hours.
result: Intensive treatment worsened the 90-day ordinal mRS outcome (common OR for worse outcome 1.37; 95% CI 1.07–1.76) and increased early neurological deterioration (common OR 1.53; 95% CI 1.18–1.97). Symptomatic ICH and mortality did not differ significantly.
limits: Stopped early for efficacy/safety concerns. These are selected successfully reperfused patients; neither the comparator nor this result establishes one BP target for every reperfusion grade or clinical situation.

title: OPTIMAL-BP — functional outcomes after post-EVT BP reduction
headline: Post-EVT SBP <140: mRS 0–2 39.4 vs 54.4%
question: Did SBP <140 improve function after successful EVT?
population: 306 randomized patients with large-vessel ischemic stroke and mTICI ≥2b reperfusion at 19 South Korean centers; 305 were confirmed eligible.
comparison: SBP <140 versus 140–180 mmHg for 24 hours after enrollment.
result: Three-month independence (mRS 0–2) was 39.4% versus 54.4% (adjusted OR 0.56; 95% CI 0.33–0.96). Symptomatic ICH was 9.0% versus 8.1%; the difference was not significant. Stroke-related death was 7.7% versus 5.4%, also not significantly different.
limits: Stopped early for safety concerns. The result concerns the tested lowering strategy after successful reperfusion; it does not establish a universal target for unsuccessful EVT or individualized reperfusion-guided management.

title: HOPE (post-EVT BP) — reperfusion-guided blood pressure targets
headline: Reperfusion-guided SBP: mRS 0–2 60.0 vs 47.1%
question: Do reperfusion-guided SBP targets after successful EVT improve outcome?
population: 440 patients with anterior LVO and mTICI ≥2b after EVT at 11 Spanish centers (mean age 75).
comparison: SBP 140–160 for mTICI 2b or 100–140 for 2c/3 for 72 hours versus SBP <180.
result: mRS 0–2 at 90 days occurred in 60.0% vs 47.1% (difference 13.3 points; 95% CI 4.1–22.6). Hemorrhagic transformation 22.3% vs 31.6%; symptomatic ICH 3.5% vs 3.9%; mortality 15.4% vs 15.6% (abstract figures).
limits: Open-label single-country trial (446 enrolled, 440 analyzed); it tests the combined strategy rather than each target. Mortality figures are from the abstract narrative.

title: INTERACT4 — ambulance BP lowering in undifferentiated stroke
headline: Prehospital SBP lowering: overall neutral; harm in ischemic stroke (cOR 1.30)
question: Does ambulance-delivered BP lowering improve outcome in suspected acute stroke?
population: 2,404 Chinese patients with a motor deficit and SBP ≥150 within 2 hours; 46.5% of confirmed strokes were hemorrhagic.
comparison: Immediate lowering to SBP 130–140 versus usual care.
result: No overall difference in 90-day mRS (cOR 1.00; 95% CI 0.87–1.15). Hemorrhagic stroke: cOR 0.75 (0.60–0.92); ischemic stroke: cOR 1.30 (1.06–1.60), i.e., worse outcome.
limits: Subgroup effects by stroke type; a very high hemorrhage proportion limits transfer to other regions.

title: CLOTS 3 — intermittent pneumatic compression after stroke
headline: IPC: proximal DVT 8.5 vs 12.1%
question: Did intermittent pneumatic compression reduce proximal DVT?
population: 2,876 acute stroke patients unable to walk to the toilet without another person’s help, enrolled during admission days 0–3 at 94 UK centers.
comparison: Intermittent pneumatic compression plus routine care versus no IPC.
result: Proximal DVT, detected by screening ultrasound or symptomatic imaging within 30 days, occurred in 8.5% versus 12.1% (absolute reduction 3.6 percentage points; 95% CI 1.4–5.8). Skin breaks were more frequent with IPC: 3% versus 1%. The 30-day mortality difference was not statistically significant.
limits: The endpoint includes asymptomatic DVT. This evaluates IPC rather than graduated compression stockings; device suitability and skin monitoring remain important.

title: FOOD — PEG versus nasogastric feeding after stroke
headline: PEG vs nasogastric: more death or poor outcome (+7.8 points)
question: Should PEG routinely replace nasogastric feeding early after stroke?
population: 321 dysphagic stroke patients in the feeding-route randomization at 47 hospitals in 11 countries.
comparison: Percutaneous endoscopic gastrostomy (PEG) versus nasogastric feeding.
result: At six months, PEG increased death or poor outcome by 7.8 percentage points (95% CI 0.0–15.5; P=0.05). The mortality difference alone was 1.0 percentage point higher with PEG (95% CI −10.0 to 11.9), without statistical significance.
limits: The report contains a separate early-versus-delayed feeding trial; do not mix its population or outcomes with this route comparison. The results do not establish that later PEG for persistent dysphagia is never appropriate.

title: SHINE — intensive glucose control in acute ischemic stroke
headline: Intensive insulin: no benefit; severe hypoglycemia 2.6%
question: Did intensive insulin treatment improve 90-day function?
population: 1,151 adults with hyperglycemic ischemic stroke enrolled within 12 hours at 63 US sites.
comparison: IV insulin targeting glucose 80–130 mg/dL versus subcutaneous sliding-scale insulin targeting 80–179 mg/dL for up to 72 hours.
result: Severity-adjusted favorable 90-day mRS outcome occurred in 20.5% versus 21.6% (adjusted RR 0.97; 95% CI 0.87–1.08). Severe hypoglycemia occurred only with intensive treatment: 15 patients (2.6%).
limits: Stopped for futility. The outcome threshold depended on baseline stroke severity. Failure of this intensive strategy does not support leaving marked hyperglycemia untreated or attributing QASC’s bundle benefit to tight glucose control.

title: QASC — implementing fever, glucose and swallowing care
headline: Nurse fever/glucose/swallow protocols: death or dependency 42 vs 58%
question: Did organized implementation improve stroke-unit outcomes?
population: 19 Australian stroke units, with 687 patients before and 1,009 after implementation; adults with ischemic stroke or ICH presenting within 48 hours.
comparison: Nurse-initiated fever, glucose and swallowing protocols plus multidisciplinary implementation workshops versus abridged guideline provision; units were randomized.
result: At 90 days, death or dependency (mRS ≥2) was 42% versus 58% in post-intervention cohorts (adjusted absolute difference 15.7 percentage points; 95% CI 5.8–25.4). Mortality alone did not differ significantly.
limits: Cluster randomization and pre/post cohorts differ from individual patient randomization. This supports implementation of the package; it cannot isolate which component produced benefit or establish an intensive glucose target.

title: DESTINY II — hemicraniectomy in older patients
headline: Hemicraniectomy 61–82 y: survival with mRS 0–4 38 vs 18%
question: What survival and disability tradeoff accompanied surgery after age 60?
population: 112 patients aged 61–82 with malignant middle-cerebral-artery infarction, randomized within 48 hours; median age 70.
comparison: Hemicraniectomy versus conservative intensive-care treatment.
result: At six months, survival with mRS 0–4 was 38% versus 18% (OR 2.91; 95% CI 1.06–7.49). Mortality was 33% versus 70%. No participant achieved mRS 0–2; most survivors needed help with bodily needs. Infections were more frequent after surgery.
limits: The primary endpoint included mRS 4 and must not be described as functional independence. Discuss the full disability distribution and the person’s acceptable outcomes; age alone is not a complete selection rule.

title: RESTART — antiplatelet therapy after antithrombotic-associated ICH
headline: Antiplatelet restart after ICH: recurrent ICH 4 vs 9% (NS)
question: Did restarting antiplatelet therapy increase recurrent ICH?
population: 537 ICH survivors previously taking antithrombotic therapy for occlusive vascular disease; randomized a median of 76 days after ICH.
comparison: Start versus avoid antiplatelet therapy.
result: Over a median two years, recurrent symptomatic ICH occurred in 12/268 (4%) versus 23/268 (9%) (adjusted HR 0.51; 95% CI 0.25–1.03). Major hemorrhagic events were 7% versus 9%; major occlusive events were 15% versus 14%, without significant differences.
limits: The confidence interval does not prove antiplatelets prevent recurrent ICH. This selected survivor cohort does not establish immediate restart timing, safety for every CAA phenotype, or anticoagulant resumption.

title: EARLYDRAIN — lumbar CSF drainage after secured aSAH
headline: Lumbar drain after aSAH: mRS 3–6 32.6 vs 44.8%
question: Did early lumbar drainage improve outcome after aneurysm treatment?
population: 287 analyzable adults with aneurysmal SAH across clinical grades; aneurysms were clipped or coiled within 48 hours.
comparison: Additional lumbar drainage at 5 mL/hour, begun within 72 hours, versus standard care.
result: Six-month mRS 3–6 occurred in 32.6% versus 44.8% (RR 0.73; 95% CI 0.52–0.98). Secondary infarction at discharge was 28.5% versus 39.9%. Drain complications included a pressure gradient stopping drainage, local infection and a retained torn catheter.
limits: Lumbar-drain contraindications included absent/compressed basal cisterns and therapeutic anticoagulation. Use the full neurosurgical drainage and pressure-monitoring protocol; this was not unrestricted drainage for every SAH presentation.

title: SAHaRA — liberal versus restrictive transfusion in aSAH
headline: Liberal transfusion in aSAH: no benefit (33.5 vs 37.7%)
question: Did a more liberal transfusion threshold improve neurological outcome?
population: 742 critically ill adults with acute aneurysmal SAH and anemia at 23 centers; 725 contributed to the primary analysis.
comparison: Mandatory red-cell transfusion at hemoglobin ≤10 g/dL versus optional transfusion at ≤8 g/dL.
result: At 12 months, unfavorable outcome (mRS ≥4) occurred in 33.5% versus 37.7% (RR 0.88; 95% CI 0.72–1.09; P=0.22). Functional-independence and quality-of-life measures did not show significant differences; adverse-event incidence was similar.
limits: No superiority was demonstrated; the confidence interval does not establish equivalence. The restrictive strategy allowed clinical discretion and must not be recast as mandatory transfusion at 8 g/dL or a universal rule for all acute brain injuries.

title: CADISS — antiplatelet versus anticoagulant treatment for dissection
headline: Dissection: antiplatelet vs anticoagulant, few events (3 vs 1)
question: Did antithrombotic strategy alter early stroke recurrence?
population: 250 patients with symptomatic extracranial carotid or vertebral dissection within seven days; central imaging review did not confirm dissection in 52.
comparison: Clinician-selected antiplatelet versus anticoagulant treatment for three months.
result: Ipsilateral stroke or death occurred in 3/126 versus 1/124 patients (P=0.63); there were no deaths. One major bleed, a subarachnoid hemorrhage, occurred with anticoagulation.
limits: Very few events and wide uncertainty prevent an equivalence conclusion. This extracranial-dissection study does not settle intracranial dissection management or which individual drug is best; consider it alongside TREAT-CAD.

title: RESPECT — PFO closure, extended follow-up
headline: PFO closure: recurrent stroke HR 0.55 over 5.9 years
question: Does PFO closure reduce recurrent stroke after cryptogenic stroke over long-term follow-up?
population: 980 patients aged 18–60 with PFO and cryptogenic ischemic stroke (mean age 45.9), followed a median 5.9 years.
comparison: PFO closure versus medical therapy (antiplatelet or warfarin).
result: Recurrent ischemic stroke 0.58 vs 1.07 per 100 patient-years (HR 0.55; 95% CI 0.31–0.999); stroke of undetermined cause HR 0.38 (0.18–0.79). Venous thromboembolism was more common with closure.
limits: Extended follow-up analysis was exploratory; unequal dropout between groups.

title: TO-ACT — endovascular treatment for severe CVT
headline: Severe CVT EVT: no benefit (mRS 0–1 67 vs 68%)
question: Did adding EVT improve outcome in severe CVT?
population: 67 adults with CVT and at least one poor-outcome risk feature: mental-status change, coma, ICH or deep cerebral venous thrombosis.
comparison: Mechanical thrombectomy and/or local thrombolysis plus medical care versus medical care alone; EVT within 24 hours of randomization.
result: At 12 months, mRS 0–1 occurred in 67% versus 68% (RR 0.99; 95% CI 0.71–1.38). Mortality was 12% versus 3% and symptomatic ICH 3% versus 9%; neither difference was significant.
limits: Stopped early for futility and too small to exclude important benefit or harm. Mixed endovascular techniques and selected severe CVT limit extrapolation; the trial does not establish routine EVT or resolve every rescue situation.

title: RE-SPECT CVT — dabigatran versus warfarin for cerebral venous thrombosis
headline: CVT: no recurrent VTE; major bleeding 1.7 vs 3.3%
question: Is dabigatran as safe and effective as warfarin after CVT?
population: 120 adults with acute CVT, stable after 5–15 days of parenteral heparin; ICH from the CVT was allowed.
comparison: Dabigatran 150 mg twice daily versus dose-adjusted warfarin for 24 weeks.
result: No recurrent venous thromboembolism in either group. Major bleeding 1.7% (1, intestinal) vs 3.3% (2, intracranial); recanalization 60.0% vs 67.3%.
limits: Small exploratory open-label trial with blinded adjudication.
